title: Office Manager Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)
meta_description: A complete office manager resume example: budgets, vendors, facilities, onboarding, and the exact bullet formula that turns keeping an office running into proof hiring managers and applicant tracking systems both reward.
content_html:
Office Manager Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

An office manager resume has one job: prove you can run an office, not just work in one. Hiring managers do not hire for task lists, software inventories, or pleasant adjectives alone. They hire for budgets held, vendors managed, facilities kept running, and new hires onboarded smoothly: the responsibility you held, the action you took, and the result that followed.

Quick answer: An office manager resume should include a summary naming the size of the office you ran and your strongest operations result, a skills section with budget management, vendor coordination, facilities management, and onboarding, experience bullets pairing each responsibility with the money saved, process fixed, or team supported, and proof of ownership through systems you built.

Key Takeaways

  • Every experience bullet follows the same formula: responsibility + action + result — the budget you held, the vendor you renegotiated, the onboarding system you built.
  • Lead with the size of the office you ran and your headline operations result: a 60-person office, a six-figure budget, onboarding cut from days to hours.
  • Spell tools exactly as postings do — Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, QuickBooks, Slack, Asana — they are literal ATS keyword filters.
  • Show impact through percentages and ranges, never through confidential figures: name the result, withhold the private detail.
  • Keep the file itself single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Ask a hiring manager what separates a keep-forever office manager from a risky one and it won’t be “highly organised.” It’ll be:

  • Budgets that hold. Spending tracked, variances caught early, and costs cut without cutting the service the team depends on.
  • Vendors that deliver. Contracts negotiated, suppliers held to their promises, and problems solved before the office notices them.
  • Facilities that just work. Space planned, maintenance scheduled, and disruptions handled quietly so work never stops.
  • Onboarding that sticks. New hires welcomed, equipped, and productive on day one, with a process that runs the same way every time.
  • Teams that stay supported. Schedules coordinated, supplies always stocked, and the hundred small things handled before anyone has to ask.

Office Manager Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is an example for an office manager running a 60-person office. It’s fictional — names and companies are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: responsibility, action, result.

DANIEL OSEI
Chicago · (312) 555-0183 · daniel.osei@email.com · linkedin.com/in/danielosei

SUMMARY
Office manager with 7 years running offices of 25 to 60 people, currently managing a 60-person office and a six-figure annual budget. Cut vendor spending by 22%, rebuilt onboarding from 3 days to 1, and eliminated supply stockouts entirely. Known for calm under pressure and offices that run themselves.

SKILLS
Budget management · Vendor coordination · Facilities management · Onboarding · Scheduling · Inventory control · Google Workspace · Microsoft 365 · Slack · Asana · Zoom · QuickBooks · Expensify · Event planning · Health and safety compliance

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Office Manager — Brightfield Consulting, Chicago | 2020–Present

  • Run daily operations for a 60-person office on a six-figure annual budget: spending tracked weekly, variances flagged early, and vendor costs cut by 22% with no drop in service.
  • Renegotiated contracts with 8 core vendors, consolidating suppliers and standardising orders to save a fifth of annual spend while improving delivery times.
  • Rebuilt onboarding from a 3-day scramble into a 1-day process: checklists, equipment ready before arrival, and a buddy system that cut new-hire setup questions by half.
  • Manage facilities for 2 floors, scheduling maintenance, safety checks, and repairs so downtime dropped to zero unplanned closures in 2 years.
  • Coordinate calendars and meeting rooms for 6 teams, ending double-bookings entirely by introducing a shared booking system the whole office now uses.
  • Run the annual office move and refit for 60 staff, delivered on budget with no lost working days, including IT setup and vendor coordination.

Office Coordinator — Halcyon Legal Group, Chicago | 2017–2020

  • Kept a 25-person office running day to day — supplies, scheduling, and vendor liaison — the work that led into an office manager role.
  • Took over supply ordering and cut stockouts from monthly occurrences to none in a year by introducing par levels and a standing order system.
  • Supported 4 partners with travel and meeting logistics, coordinating rooms and materials for up to 30 attendees so partners walked in ready.
  • Handled reception cover and front-of-house duties, greeting clients and managing the first impression of the firm.

EDUCATION
BA, Business Administration — 2017

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: office size, tenure, and headline proof in three lines

The example opens with office size and tenure, then the proof: vendor spending cut, onboarding rebuilt, stockouts eliminated. Without office manager experience yet, lead with equivalent scope: “ran daily operations for a 25-person office, including vendor scheduling and new-hire onboarding.”

Skills: tools and duties exactly as postings spell them

Office operations postings are keyword-dense, and applicant tracking systems screen for exact terms. Name your tools (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, QuickBooks) and your duties (budget management, vendor coordination, facilities management). “Great organiser” is not a keyword; “budget management” is.

Experience: every bullet pairs a responsibility with the result gained

The pattern is responsibility + action + result: “cut vendor spending by 22% by consolidating suppliers”; “rebuilt onboarding from 3 days to 1 with checklists and ready equipment.” Scope matters too — people supported, budget held, vendors managed, floors maintained.

Impact: show it through percentages and ranges, never through secrets

Every office manager claims impact; the strong ones prove it by naming the result and withholding the confidential detail: spending cut by a fifth, onboarding halved, stockouts eliminated. One bullet about a budget held or a system built proves the ownership hiring managers pay for, and separates an office manager resume from a task list.

Office Manager Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s exact language and keep these groups on your resume:

  • Budget & procurement: budget management, vendor coordination, procurement, expense tracking, QuickBooks, Expensify (only the depth you genuinely have).
  • Facilities & operations: facilities management, space planning, maintenance scheduling, health and safety compliance, inventory control.
  • People & onboarding: onboarding, scheduling, team coordination, meeting coordination, event planning, reception.
  • Tools: Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Asana, Zoom, QuickBooks, Microsoft Office.

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Office manager resumes fail most often on vague bullets and missing keywords, not on formatting. Start from a clean template gallery or resume builder option, then verify with the free ATS grader.

5 Mistakes That Cost Office Manager Interviews

  1. Task lists instead of ownership. “Ordered supplies and answered phones” says nothing about the office you ran. Every bullet needs a responsibility, an action, and a result.
  2. Confidential figures dressed as proof. Naming exact budgets, salaries, or contract prices to sound important breaks the very trust the role requires. Use percentages and ranges instead.
  3. Vague operations language. “Managed the office” and “handled administration” mean nothing to a hiring manager. Name the size, the systems, and the result: budget held, vendor renegotiated, onboarding rebuilt.
  4. Tools without matching bullets. A software list proves nothing on its own. Pair each tool with work that used it: the budget tracked, the vendor paid, the onboarding run.
  5. Unreadable formatting. Multi-column layouts, text boxes, and image-based PDFs scramble parsing, so your budget-management section arrives as word soup. One column, standard headings, real text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in an office manager resume?

A summary naming the size of the office you ran and your strongest operations result; a skills section with budget management, vendor coordination, facilities management, and onboarding; experience bullets pairing each responsibility with the money saved, process fixed, or team supported; and proof of ownership through systems you built, never through vague claims of being organised. Running an office beats listing office tasks alone.

Do I need a degree to become an office manager?

Not always — office managers come from administrative support, reception, customer service, hospitality, and executive assistance, and many enter through an administrative role plus a record of keeping an office running. Hiring managers weigh the size of the office you ran and the problems you solved far more than a specific degree. A business or management degree helps for some employers, but a budget held, a vendor renegotiated, and an onboarding system built prove more.

How do I show office manager impact without revealing company finances?

Use percentages and ranges instead of exact figures: “cut vendor spending by 22%” or “managed an annual office budget of six figures” proves impact without disclosing anything private. Never name suppliers’ prices, salaries, or contract terms that were not public. Recruiters read impact as a skill: the result stated plainly, the confidential detail withheld, and the scale implied by the office itself.

What is the difference between an office manager and an administrative assistant resume?

An administrative assistant resume proves reliable support: scheduling, correspondence, supplies, and day-to-day coordination. An office manager resume proves ownership of the office itself: the budget, the vendors, the facilities, the onboarding, and the team that keeps it all running. The office manager resume names the office size and the systems built; the administrative resume names the tasks completed.

How do I write an office manager resume with no office manager title yet?

Lead with the closest equivalent work: the office you kept running, the vendors you coordinated, the supplies you ordered, the onboarding you ran, or the team you scheduled — then frame each as office management in miniature. “Ran daily operations for a 25-person office, including vendor scheduling and new-hire onboarding” proves the same skills at smaller scale. Add relevant software, run it through a free ATS grader first, and target office coordinator or operations assistant roles as stepping stones.

Should an office manager resume list software tools?

Yes — tool keywords are literal ATS filters in office operations roles. List scheduling and office tools (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365), finance and procurement systems (QuickBooks, Expensify), and coordination tools (Slack, Asana, Zoom) exactly as postings spell them, and only tools you genuinely use. A tool without a matching bullet reads thin, so pair each one with work that used it: the budget tracked, the vendor paid, the onboarding run.
